Conor Williams: Williams has the physical profile and tape of a franchise left tackle. The highly regarded Texas recruit looks capable of holding down the blind side for a decade, making him the early standard for offensive linemen in this class as scouts return to the tape.
James Rodriquez: Rodriquez pairs a 6-foot-5 frame with elite instincts and the athleticism to cover ground for Ohio State. The former five-star has produced every year and shows the feel to handle zone assignments. He has the tools to organize a defense and influence plays on all three downs.
Mikael Thomas: Thomas reads throws early and has the range to close on them from zone coverage. The Clemson corner pairs those instincts with elite ball skills, giving him a chance to turn a contested pass into a takeaway. That combination puts him among the class’s premier coverage prospects.
Jordan Nunez: Nunez gives Notre Dame a 6-foot-8, 320-pound tackle with the strength to control defenders on contact. His ability to play on either side adds rare flexibility to that imposing physical profile. He enters the year with the tools to become a franchise bookend on an offensive line.
Neville Gibson: Gibson pairs punishing hits with the ball skills to finish interceptions, giving Ohio State a safety who can influence plays all over the field. The former five-star captains a talented defense and brings the leadership and playmaking to project as a cornerstone of a secondary.
Ryan Hodges III: Hodges returned to Ohio State with a chance to raise his draft stock. His soft hands and unusually large catch radius help him make difficult grabs look routine, giving quarterbacks room to throw even when the window appears tight or the ball arrives off target.
Taylen Ingram: Ingram gives Florida a receiver with blazing vertical speed and the creativity to keep making plays once the ball reaches him. His contact balance helps him stay on his feet through the first hit. He can threaten a defense both downfield and on touches in space.
Brennan Coombs: Coombs approaches defense like a quarterback, using his understanding of the game to direct the players around him. The Texas A&M standout enters the season among the nation’s top linebackers and has the leadership profile to take charge of a defense early in his career.
Matteo Jackson: Jackson builds speed smoothly with long strides and gives USC a receiver who can work from different spots in the formation. His strong hands help him finish catches when the ball reaches him. The combination gives him a chance to turn clean releases into explosive plays.
Alex Martinez: Martinez led Ohio State in touchdown catches in his first year as a starter. The former five-star recruit brings the athleticism to be a featured target at tight end, and that early production gives him a strong base heading into the season.
Troy Morales: Morales gives Oregon a long corner who can play close to the line and stay with receivers through their breaks. His hips turn smoothly for a player with his frame, and he competes through the route. Those traits give him a plausible starting role on the boundary.
Bo Weatherly: Weatherly gives Tennessee a 6-foot-6 target who can stretch the seam with long strides. His catch radius opens throwing windows above defenders and makes him a matchup problem inside. Quarterbacks can use that reach to attack parts of the field where smaller targets have less room.
Bryan Nunez: Nunez sees lanes develop and has the footwork to change direction before defenders can close them. The Clemson runner can turn a small opening into a bigger gain with his burst and creativity. Those traits are especially apparent when he gets room to work in the open field.
Coleton Williamson: Williamson gives Alabama a right tackle who can win with sound technique. He sets his feet steadily and uses strong hands to control the initial contact. That combination of footwork and strength offers a strong starting foundation on the right side of a professional line.
Chuma Okar: Okar gets off the ball quickly enough to put an offensive tackle on the defensive from the snap. The Oklahoma edge rusher shows a feel for finding his way into the backfield. His first step is the clearest reason to watch how his pass rush develops.
Khalil Miller: Miller brings unusual burst for an interior defender of his size and can get upfield before a blocker settles. His hands give him another way to clear contact. That mix of first-step speed and power gives LSU a tackle capable of disrupting plays from inside.
Alex Savage: Savage accelerates quickly off the edge and takes sharp angles when the ball moves away from him. Georgia can use that pursuit speed on downs when he has room to build momentum. The same quickness gives him a foundation to develop as a pass rusher.
Deandre Muncy: Muncy diagnoses runs and steps downhill with the physicality to finish tackles for Texas. His instincts and reliable tackling give him a clear role against the run. Those strengths form the foundation of a linebacker with the potential to stay on the field for all three downs.
C.J. Nielsen: Nielsen opens the season as the leading quarterback prospect on the board. The 6-foot-4 Ole Miss passer works comfortably from the pocket and throws with anticipation, giving receivers a chance to meet the ball as they break. His size and timing give him the profile of a starter.
Jonathan Pickney: Pickney gives Alabama a 331-pound tackle with a sturdy anchor against power. He brings imposing strength to the run game and can create movement when he gets his hands on a defender. His best work is on assignments that let him plant and drive through contact.
Shayne Crawford: Crawford brings long limbs and building speed to the edge for Kansas. He can cover ground quickly once he opens his stride, giving him a chance to turn pursuit into pressure. His length lets him close the final space between himself and a quarterback on the move.
Joseph Simmons: Simmons uses quick hands and good leverage to attack interior gaps before blockers settle. The Mississippi State tackle stays active through the play, giving the front a chance to disrupt a run or pressure the passer. His best work comes when he can penetrate and keep moving.
Tyquavion Jones: Jones reads routes quickly in zone and reacts when a throw comes into his area. The Ohio State corner uses that recognition to get himself in position for a play on the ball. His instincts give him a chance to turn late throws into takeaways.
Justin Okpara: Okpara arrived at Louisville from Washington after entering college as a five-star recruit and the top quarterback in his class. His quick feet help him escape crowded pockets and extend plays. That ability to improvise gives the offense chances to create when the play moves outside its original design.
Treyton Britt: Britt gives Tulsa a tall safety with the range to work across the deep middle. His anticipation helps him get a head start on the throw, and his length gives him a chance to finish interceptions. Those traits make him an intriguing center-field prospect.
Johnny Hatcher: Hatcher gives South Carolina a heavy-handed edge defender who can push a tackle back with his bull rush. His size and strength let him dictate the first collision. That power is his clearest path to pressure when he can get square to the blocker.
Sammy Mosley: Mosley moves fluidly in coverage and has the awareness to pick up routes as they develop. His pursuit speed helps him close space for Clemson after the ball comes out. Those traits give him a role on passing downs that can carry beyond a single matchup.
Jocquise Harrison: Harrison gives Ohio State a long slot corner who can react quickly and use contact to stay connected to a route. His size creates options against different inside targets. That flexibility is worth watching when the offense moves receivers around before the snap to create matchups.
DaQuan Jefferson: Jefferson anchors Alabama’s interior front with heavy hands and the strength to hold his gap. He can make it difficult for a blocker to move him off the spot, giving the defense a reliable presence against the run. His early value starts with controlling space inside.
Joziah Brooks: Brooks gives Oregon a 334-pound guard who can drive defenders out of a running lane. His size and strength also help him hold his ground when a rusher attacks through him. That combination gives him a direct role on an interior line built to create movement.
Troy Redman: Redman brings strong hands and forceful contact to the edge for Ohio State. He can use that power to move a blocker backward and tighten the pocket. His clearest route to pressure comes when he gets his hands inside and keeps driving through the tackle.
Ayren Leonard: Leonard gives LSU a long edge rusher who accelerates quickly and bends around the outside shoulder of a tackle. His length lets him finish when he gets even with the blocker. That combination makes him a player to watch for a breakout as a pass rusher.
